Provides Dunnett's T3 Simultaneous Confidence Intervals for All Pairwise Comparisons Without Assuming Homogeneity of Variance

Source: R/ci_dunnett_t3.R
ci_dunnett_t3.Rd

Forms simultaneous confidence intervals and multiplicity-adjusted p-values for all \(a(a-1)/2\) pairwise differences among \(a\) group means without assuming that the groups share a variance. Each pair has its own standard error and Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, and its critical value is that of the studentized maximum modulus for the \(a(a-1)/2\) comparisons at those degrees of freedom (Dunnett, 1980). This is the procedure SPSS reports as Dunnett's T3; cv_smm gives its critical value.

Usage

ci_dunnett_t3(x, group = NULL, conf_level = 0.95)

Arguments

x

Either (a) a fitted lm or aov object with a single factor predictor, or (b) a numeric vector of the outcome, in which case group must also be supplied. An infinite outcome value is an error, since it leaves its group's mean and variance undefined.

group

When x is a vector, a factor (or coercible to factor) giving the group membership of each observation. Observations with a missing outcome or a missing group are dropped.

conf_level

Family-wise confidence level. Default 0.95.

Value

A data.frame with one row per pairwise comparison, in the order ci_games_howell uses: with the factor levels in their order, each later level is compared with each earlier one, and the contrast label ("B - A") names the difference taken. The columns are contrast, mean_difference, se (the separate-variance standard error of the difference), df (the pair's Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, which is why it varies from row to row), t_value (mean_difference divided by se), ci_lower, ci_upper, and p_adjusted. The conf_level attribute records the family-wise level, and the ci_adjustment and p_adjustment attributes are "dunnett_t3". The table prints through the dmar_tbl display layer and works with tidy and glance (see dmar_tidiers).

Details

The procedure. For groups \(g\) and \(h\), with means \(\bar Y_g\) and \(\bar Y_h\), variances \(s_g^2\) and \(s_h^2\), and sizes \(n_g\) and \(n_h\), the standard error of the difference uses only those two groups' variances, $$\mathit{SE}_{gh} = \sqrt{s_g^2/n_g + s_h^2/n_h},$$ and its degrees of freedom are the Welch–Satterthwaite value $$\mathit{df}_{gh} = \frac{(s_g^2/n_g + s_h^2/n_h)^2}{s_g^4/[n_g^2(n_g-1)] + s_h^4/[n_h^2(n_h-1)]},$$ as in Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027, Equations 5.13 and 5.14) and in base R's t.test for two groups. With \(C = a(a-1)/2\) comparisons in the family and \(\alpha\) equal to one minus conf_level, the interval for \(\mu_h - \mu_g\) is $$(\bar Y_h - \bar Y_g) \pm m_{\alpha;\,C,\,\mathit{df}_{gh}}\,\mathit{SE}_{gh},$$ where \(m_{\alpha;C,\mathit{df}}\) is the upper \(\alpha\) critical value of the studentized maximum modulus for \(C\) comparisons on \(\mathit{df}\) degrees of freedom (Stoline & Ury, 1979), the value cv_smm(alpha_level = 1 - conf_level, df, n_comparisons = C) returns. The adjusted p-value is the probability that a studentized maximum modulus variate for \(C\) comparisons on the pair's degrees of freedom exceeds the observed \(|t| = |\bar Y_h - \bar Y_g| / \mathit{SE}_{gh}\), so a pair's p_adjusted falls below \(\alpha\) when its interval excludes zero and not otherwise, to numerical precision: the critical value's tail area matches \(\alpha\) to a relative \(10^{-6}\) or better. Both are computed by numerical integration rather than simulation, and the degrees of freedom are not rounded. As with Games–Howell, the family-wise level holds approximately rather than exactly, since each pair is referred to a distribution indexed by its own estimated degrees of freedom.

Dunnett's T3 and Tamhane's T2. Tamhane (1979) compared procedures for pairwise comparisons of means with unequal variances. The one known as Tamhane's T2 uses the same standard errors and degrees of freedom but takes its critical value from the inequality of Šidák (1967), treating the \(C\) t statistics as if they were independent: each pair is tested at the level \(1 - (1 - \alpha)^{1/C}\), so its critical value is the \((1 + (1 - \alpha)^{1/C})/2\) quantile of t on \(\mathit{df}_{gh}\) and its adjusted p-value is \(1 - (1 - p_{gh})^C\), with \(p_{gh}\) the pair's two-sided Welch p-value. Dunnett (1980) replaced that bound with the studentized maximum modulus at the same degrees of freedom. The two distribution functions differ only in where the power is taken. With \(S = \sqrt{\chi^2_{\mathit{df}}/\mathit{df}}\) and \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function, the probability that all \(C\) statistics fall within \(\pm c\) is \(\{\mathrm{E}[2\Phi(cS) - 1]\}^C\) as T2 computes it and \(\mathrm{E}\{[2\Phi(cS) - 1]^C\}\) under the studentized maximum modulus, which by Jensen's inequality is never the smaller of the two. T3's critical value therefore never exceeds T2's at the same degrees of freedom: its intervals are never wider, and its adjusted p-values never larger. On the reactivated-story scores of Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027, Chapter 12, Exercise 25), three groups of 13, the T2 p-values are .045, .001, and .027 and the T3 values .044, .001, and .026, which are the values SPSS reports for Dunnett's T3. SPSS offers the two as separate procedures, Tamhane's T2 and Dunnett's T3; the T in T3 comes from Tamhane, who developed its predecessor (Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley, 2027, Chapter 5). A formula that raises the single t probability \(2F_t(|t|) - 1\), with \(F_t\) the distribution function of t on \(\mathit{df}_{gh}\), to the power \(C\) computes T2, whatever it is called.

Dunnett's T3 or Games–Howell. ci_games_howell uses the same standard errors and degrees of freedom but refers \(|t|\sqrt{2}\) to the studentized range for \(a\) means. Dunnett (1980) found that Games–Howell becomes slightly liberal when the samples are small, and Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027, Chapter 5) therefore recommend Dunnett's T3 when the groups have fewer than roughly 50 observations each and Games–Howell for larger samples. When the variances are in fact homogeneous, ci_tukey_kramer pools them and so has more error degrees of freedom and more power. With two groups the T3 interval and p-value are exactly those of Welch's t test, t.test(..., var.equal = FALSE), because the studentized maximum modulus for one comparison is the two-sided t.

References

Dunnett, C. W. (1980). Pairwise multiple comparisons in the unequal variance case. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 75(372), 796–800. doi:10.2307/2287161

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 5 on the multiple-comparisons problem, where the modifications of Tukey's HSD for unequal variances, Dunnett's T3 and Games–Howell, are developed.)

Šidák, Z. (1967). Rectangular confidence regions for the means of multivariate normal distributions. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 62(318), 626–633. doi:10.1080/01621459.1967.10482935

Stoline, M. R., & Ury, H. K. (1979). Tables of the Studentized maximum modulus distribution and an application to multiple comparisons among means. Technometrics, 21(1), 87–93. doi:10.1080/00401706.1979.10489726

Tamhane, A. C. (1979). A comparison of procedures for multiple comparisons of means with unequal variances. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 74(366), 471–480. doi:10.2307/2286358

See also

cv_smm for the critical value it uses, ci_games_howell for the studentized range counterpart, ci_tukey_kramer for the homogeneity-assuming counterpart, ci_dunnett for many-to-one comparisons, and dmar_tidiers for the tidy methods.

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# The raw drinks_per_week outcome of the drinks_trial data: the arms hold
# 37, 32, and 19 patients, fewer than the roughly 50 per group below
# which Games-Howell runs slightly liberal, and the Standard arm's
# variance is more than three times that of either CRA arm.
ci_dunnett_t3(drinks_trial$drinks_per_week, drinks_trial$treatment)
#>  contrast                    mean_difference se     df     t_value ci_lower
#>  CRA - Standard              -24.474         20.108 56.392 -1.217  -73.898 
#>  CRA + Disulfiram - Standard -24.690         22.363 53.210 -1.104  -79.753 
#>  CRA + Disulfiram - CRA      -0.216          17.178 35.653 -0.013  -43.164 
#>  ci_upper p_adjusted
#>  24.950   0.5366    
#>  30.373   0.6135    
#>  42.732   1.0000    
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%, simultaneous interval (Dunnett's T3)

# A fitted one-way model may be passed instead of the two vectors.
ci_dunnett_t3(aov(drinks_per_week ~ treatment, data = drinks_trial))
#>  contrast                    mean_difference se     df     t_value ci_lower
#>  CRA - Standard              -24.474         20.108 56.392 -1.217  -73.898 
#>  CRA + Disulfiram - Standard -24.690         22.363 53.210 -1.104  -79.753 
#>  CRA + Disulfiram - CRA      -0.216          17.178 35.653 -0.013  -43.164 
#>  ci_upper p_adjusted
#>  24.950   0.5366    
#>  30.373   0.6135    
#>  42.732   1.0000    
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%, simultaneous interval (Dunnett's T3)

# Each half-width is the studentized maximum modulus critical value for
# the three comparisons, at that pair's degrees of freedom, times the
# pair's standard error.
t3 <- ci_dunnett_t3(drinks_trial$drinks_per_week, drinks_trial$treatment)
t3$ci_upper[1] - t3$mean_difference[1]
#> [1] 49.42394
cv_smm(alpha_level = .05, df = t3$df[1], n_comparisons = 3)$value * t3$se[1]
#> [1] 49.42394
